subject: english-language
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: 'Child-directed speech' (CDS), formerly called motherese, is typically characterised by:
options: Complex subordinate clauses and rapid speech
Use of jargon and technical terms
Higher pitch, exaggerated intonation, repetition and simplified vocabulary
questions.explain: CDS features raised pitch, slower tempo, repetition and simplified syntax, thought to support acquisition.

questions.q: The 'interactional' function in Halliday's framework is used by children to:
options: Build and maintain relationships with others
questions.explain: The interactional function ('love you') develops and sustains social relationships between the child and others.

questions.q: Vygotsky's 'Zone of Proximal Development' refers to:
options: The gap between what a child can do alone and what they can achieve with support
questions.explain: The ZPD is the range of tasks a learner can accomplish with guidance from a more knowledgeable other, central to Vygotsky's social theory.

questions.q: Halliday's taxonomy of language functions includes the 'instrumental' function, which is used to:
questions.explain: In Halliday's model the instrumental function expresses needs ('want milk'), while the regulatory function controls others' behaviour.

questions.q: In phonological development, voiced sounds and front consonants like /p/, /b/, /m/ tend to be acquired:
questions.explain: Bilabial and other front consonants such as /p/, /b/, /m/ are typically among the earliest sounds children produce.

questions.q: Berko's 'wug test' demonstrated that young children can:
options: Apply grammatical rules such as plural -s to invented words
questions.explain: In Berko's study children added the plural -s to the nonsense word 'wug', showing they had internalised the rule, not merely memorised forms.

questions.q: The telegraphic stage of development is characterised by utterances that:
options: Are grammatically complete with all inflections
Use three or more words while omitting function words like determiners and auxiliaries
questions.explain: Telegraphic speech (around 24-36 months) strings content words together, e.g. 'Daddy throw ball', leaving out grammatical function words.

questions.q: The order in which children acquire grammatical morphemes (e.g. -ing before regular plural -s before past -ed) was studied by:
questions.explain: Roger Brown documented a relatively consistent order of acquisition of grammatical morphemes in young children.

questions.q: Cross-sectional and longitudinal are two designs used to study child language; a longitudinal study:
options: Tests many different children once at a single point
Follows the same child or children over an extended period
questions.explain: Longitudinal studies track the same subjects over time to chart developmental change, unlike cross-sectional snapshots.

questions.q: When a child says 'goed' instead of 'went', this is best described as:
options: Over-generalisation of a grammatical rule (a virtuous error)
questions.explain: 'Goed' shows over-generalisation of the regular past-tense rule to an irregular verb, evidence the child is applying rules rather than imitating.

questions.q: Bruner's concept of the 'Language Acquisition Support System' (LASS) refers to:
options: An innate device inside the child's brain
The supportive interaction and scaffolding provided by caregivers
questions.explain: Bruner's LASS stresses the role of adult interaction, routines and scaffolding in supporting a child's language development.

questions.q: A child who uses the word 'cup' only for their own special cup and no other cups is showing:
questions.explain: Under-extension restricts a word's meaning to fewer referents than the adult use allows.

questions.q: A key criticism of Skinner's imitation theory, raised by Chomsky, is that:
options: Children produce novel utterances they have never heard, such as 'goed'
questions.explain: The creation of forms like 'goed', never modelled by adults, suggests children apply internal rules rather than merely imitating.

questions.q: In the development of writing, Kroll's stages place which stage first?
questions.explain: Kroll's model begins with the preparatory stage (developing motor skills and the basic principles of the writing system).

questions.q: Piaget's theory links language development to:
options: The child's underlying cognitive development and stages of thought
questions.explain: Piaget argued language reflects and depends on cognitive maturation; children can only express concepts they have cognitively developed.

questions.q: During which stage of language acquisition do infants typically produce repeated consonant-vowel sounds such as 'baba' and 'gaga'?
questions.explain: Babbling (around 6-9 months) features reduplicated CV syllables, preceding the emergence of first words.

questions.q: The 'cooing' stage typically occurs at approximately:
questions.explain: Cooing, comprising open vowel-like sounds, emerges from around 6-8 weeks, before babbling begins.

questions.q: Which theorist proposed an innate 'Language Acquisition Device' (LAD)?
questions.explain: Chomsky's nativist theory argues children possess an innate LAD enabling rapid grammar acquisition from limited input.

questions.q: The 'heuristic' function in Halliday's model is used to:
options: Explore and learn about the environment, often through questions
questions.explain: The heuristic function uses language to investigate the world, frequently via 'why' and 'what' questions.

questions.q: In the post-telegraphic stage, a notable development is the appearance of:
options: Function words, inflections and more complex, grammatically complete structures
questions.explain: Post-telegraphic speech increasingly includes determiners, auxiliaries, inflections and complex/compound sentences toward adult grammar.

questions.q: The two-word stage is significant because it marks the first appearance of:
questions.explain: At the two-word stage children begin combining words in consistent order, showing early grammatical/syntactic awareness.

questions.q: Halliday's 'regulatory' function of child language is used to:
options: Influence or control the behaviour of others
questions.explain: The regulatory function gives directions to control others, e.g. 'do that again', whereas the interactional maintains relationships.

questions.q: Skinner's behaviourist account of language acquisition emphasises:
questions.explain: Skinner argued children learn language through imitation and operant conditioning, with correct utterances reinforced by carers.

questions.q: The 'holophrastic' stage of child language is so called because the child:
options: Uses a single word to express a whole idea or sentence
questions.explain: In the holophrastic (one-word) stage a single word such as 'milk' conveys a complete proposition or request.

questions.q: The phonological simplification whereby 'spoon' becomes 'poon' is called:
questions.explain: Cluster reduction simplifies consonant clusters by deleting one consonant, e.g. /sp/ reduced to /p/ in 'poon'.

questions.q: In phonological development, children often simplify pronunciation by 'reduplication', for example saying:
questions.explain: Reduplication repeats a syllable to simplify a target word, e.g. 'wawa' for 'water', a common phonological simplification process.

questions.q: A child who calls all four-legged animals 'dog' is displaying:
questions.explain: Over-extension is applying a word too broadly to include items beyond its conventional meaning.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects the nativist position on a 'critical period' for language?
options: There is a biologically optimal window in early childhood for acquiring language
Only writing has a critical period
Language can be acquired equally easily at any age
Language is purely learned through reward
questions.explain: The critical period hypothesis (associated with Lenneberg) holds that there is an early window during which language is most readily acquired.

questions.q: A 'virtuous error' is so termed because it:
options: Reveals the child applying a logical rule, even if the result is non-standard
Shows the child is morally good
questions.explain: Virtuous errors like 'sheeps' or 'runned' reflect intelligent rule application, evidencing active learning rather than careless mistakes.
